stem:
A 58-year-old man presents to a metropolitan emergency department with 3 weeks of low-grade fever, weight loss of 4 kg, and increasing dyspnoea on exertion. He had a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement 2 years ago for calcific aortic stenosis and is otherwise well. He denies any recent dental procedure but had a dental cleaning 6 weeks ago and did not receive antibiotic prophylaxis.

On examination he has a soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge and a small linear haemorrhage under his right great toenail. Splinter haemorrhages are visible on his left index finger. Three sets of blood cultures drawn 12 hours apart have all grown Streptococcus sanguinis, sensitive to benzylpenicillin. A transoesophageal echocardiogram today demonstrates a 6 mm mobile echogenic mass on the aortic side of the prosthetic aortic valve with new mild aortic regurgitation.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 96, blood pressure 110/58, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 38.2 degrees
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 108 g/L (130-180), white cell count 14 x10 to the 9 per litre (4.0-11.0), CRP 82 mg/L (less than 5), creatinine 92 micromol/L (60-110)
data_table.Blood cultures: three sets over 24 hours all positive for Streptococcus sanguinis
data_table.Echocardiography: 6 mm mobile mass on aortic side of prosthetic aortic valve, new mild aortic regurgitation

lead_in: Which of the following statements correctly categorises the modified Duke criteria met by this presentation?

options.text: This meets 1 major and 2 minor criteria only, which is insufficient for a definite diagnosis and requires a possible endocarditis classification while further criteria are sought
This meets 1 major and 4 minor criteria, which meets a definite endocarditis classification and requires no additional echocardiographic imaging at all
This meets 5 minor criteria and no major criteria, allowing a definite endocarditis diagnosis to be made once further blood culture sets are drawn to confirm
This meets neither major nor sufficient minor criteria and requires cardiac magnetic resonance imaging today before a definite classification can be applied
This meets 2 major criteria (typical organism on persistently positive blood cultures plus echocardiographic vegetation with new regurgitation), sufficient for a definite endocarditis diagnosis

subtopic_detail: COPD GOLD Group E escalation therapy
stem:
A 68-year-old man with a 40 pack-year smoking history and moderate COPD attends his general practice for review after a hospital admission for infective exacerbation 4 weeks ago requiring intravenous antibiotics. This is his second exacerbation this year, the first being managed in the community with oral prednisolone and doxycycline. Spirometry shows post-bronchodilator FEV1 of 55 percent predicted with a modified Medical Research Council dyspnoea score of 2 out of 4.

He stopped smoking during the last admission and has re-engaged with pulmonary rehabilitation. His current inhaled therapy is tiotropium 18 microgram once daily via HandiHaler alone. He reports good adherence and correct inhaler technique demonstrated at the pharmacy. His eosinophil count on the recent admission was 320 cells per microlitre (150-500) and he has no history of asthma or atopic disease.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: post-bronchodilator FEV1 55 percent predicted, mMRC 2 out of 4, peripheral eosinophil count 320 cells per microlitre
data_table.Exacerbation history: one community-managed exacerbation and one hospitalisation in the past 12 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to his inhaled therapy?

options.text: Switch tiotropium to a fixed dose LABA plus LAMA (long-acting beta-agonist plus long-acting muscarinic antagonist) combination inhaler in a single device
Continue tiotropium monotherapy and add a short-acting beta-agonist reliever only, with review in 3 months and repeat spirometry at that time
Switch immediately to triple therapy (LABA plus LAMA plus inhaled corticosteroid) as a single combination inhaler on the basis of the elevated eosinophil count
Add oral theophylline modified release 200 mg twice daily for its anti-inflammatory effect and repeat serum drug levels at 2 weeks after initiation
Commence long term oral prednisolone 5 mg daily to reduce the risk of further exacerbations over the next 12 months of maintenance treatment

stem:
A 72-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after a fall onto her head at home. She has an obvious right-sided haematoma over the temporal region and has vomited twice. On arrival her GCS is 13 (E3V4M6) and she is confused about time and place. A non-contrast CT scan of the brain shows a 15 mm right frontal intraparenchymal haemorrhage with 6 mm midline shift.

She has atrial fibrillation and takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily for stroke prevention (CHA2DS2-VA score 5). Her last dose was this morning approximately 4 hours ago. Her renal function is normal with creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90) and her weight is 68 kg. She has no other bleeding sources and no ongoing extracranial haemorrhage. Neurosurgical consultation has been sought and they advise urgent reversal is required.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 92, blood pressure 148/86, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees, GCS 13
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-165), platelets 240 x10 to the 9 per litre (150-400), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90), INR 1.1 (0.9-1.2), activated partial thromboplastin time 32 seconds (25-35)
data_table.Imaging: non-contrast CT brain with 15 mm right frontal intraparenchymal haemorrhage and 6 mm midline shift

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reversal agent?

options.text: Administer intravenous idarucizumab 5 g in two 2.5 g intravenous bolus doses within 15 minutes of each other for urgent DOAC reversal now
Administer intravenous andexanet alfa in a bolus and infusion regimen dosed per the last dose and time since ingestion of apixaban
Administer intravenous vitamin K 10 mg with 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate at 25 units/kg for warfarin-type coagulopathy reversal
Administer intravenous fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg as the first-line reversal for apixaban-associated intracerebral haemorrhage in this patient
Administer intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g bolus as monotherapy for apixaban reversal in this haemorrhagic stroke without other reversal agents

stem:
A 68-year-old woman presents to a metropolitan emergency department with 24 hours of loin pain, dysuria and fever. On arrival she is confused, cool peripherally, and has a mottled abdomen. Her past history includes type 2 diabetes on metformin and long-standing recurrent urinary tract infection. She has no known drug allergies.

On examination she has significant right renal angle tenderness and a distended bladder. Her point-of-care ultrasound shows moderate right hydronephrosis with debris in the collecting system. A urinary catheter has been placed with 300 mL of purulent urine drained on insertion. The Australian Sepsis Network hour-1 bundle has been activated. Urology have been contacted regarding potential percutaneous nephrostomy.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 128, blood pressure 78/48, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165), white cell count 18 x10 to the 9 per litre (4.0-11.0), venous lactate 4.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.2), creatinine 168 micromol/L (45-90), CRP 240 mg/L (less than 5)
data_table.Bedside investigations: catheter urine dip 4+ leukocytes, nitrites positive, moderate blood; blood glucose 12.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the correct order of the hour-1 bundle interventions?

options.text: Commence vasopressors first for hypotension, then administer broad-spectrum antibiotics, then measure lactate, then obtain cultures, then commence 30 mL/kg crystalloid resuscitation over 3 hours in a controlled ICU setting
Administer antibiotics first without cultures, then measure lactate, then commence crystalloid resuscitation at 20 mL/kg to reduce risk of pulmonary oedema, then obtain blood and urine cultures

Await urinary culture results before administering antibiotics to guide narrow-spectrum therapy, commence 30 mL/kg crystalloid, measure lactate, and consider vasopressors once organism identified in the microbiology laboratory

Measure lactate, obtain blood and urine cultures, administer broad-spectrum antibiotics (empirical piperacillin-tazobactam and gentamicin), commence 30 mL/kg crystalloid resuscitation, and start vasopressors for persistent hypotension after fluid

Perform urgent contrast CT abdomen and pelvis to identify the source, then obtain blood cultures, administer broad-spectrum antibiotics, commence 30 mL/kg crystalloid, and measure lactate after resuscitation is completed

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis in known Addison's during acute illness
stem:
A 42-year-old woman with known primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) is brought to a rural emergency department with 24 hours of vomiting from gastroenteritis. She takes hydrocortisone 15 mg on waking and 5 mg at 4 p.m., and fludrocortisone 100 microgram in the morning. She reports she doubled her hydrocortisone dose orally 12 hours ago but has vomited each subsequent dose within 30 minutes of taking it.

She is drowsy and confused. Her family confirms she has been unable to keep down fluids. There is no fever and no localising infective source apart from the gastroenteritis. She wears a medical alert bracelet identifying her as having primary adrenal insufficiency. Her partner has brought her intramuscular hydrocortisone emergency kit from home.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 128, blood pressure 74/44, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees
data_table.Investigations: sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), creatinine 118 micromol/L (45-90), venous pH 7.30
data_table.Bedside investigations: 12-lead ECG with sinus tachycardia and peaked T waves in the precordial leads

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg immediately in place of hydrocortisone and await the results of a short synacthen test performed later today at bedside
Administer intravenous calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL for hyperkalaemia and defer steroid dosing until potassium is under 5.0 mmol/L on repeat testing
Administer oral prednisolone 25 mg with an antiemetic and observe for 4 hours before deciding on intravenous replacement therapy in the resuscitation area
Administer intravenous fludrocortisone 200 microgram immediately as mineralocorticoid replacement therapy for the electrolyte disturbance in adrenal crisis
Administer intramuscular or intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately, then 200 mg over 24 hours by infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours, with concurrent saline and dextrose resuscitation

subtopic_detail: Hyponatraemia correction rate ceiling to avoid osmotic demyelination
stem:
A 78-year-old woman is admitted from a residential aged care facility with 5 days of increasing confusion after a viral gastroenteritis and 4 days of poor oral intake. She takes hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily for hypertension and citalopram 20 mg daily for depression. On admission her serum sodium is 112 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L, urea 4.8 mmol/L (3-8), and urine sodium 42 mmol/L (spot).

She is drowsy but rousable, has no seizures, and has a GCS of 12 (E3V4M5). Serum osmolality is 240 mOsm/kg (275-295) and urine osmolality is 380 mOsm/kg. She has no oedema and has an estimated 1 to 2 percent volume depletion on clinical assessment. She has no known alcohol use disorder and no history of chronic kidney disease. Family confirm the confusion has been progressive over the past 3 days.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 92, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees, GCS 12
data_table.Investigations: sodium 112 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 4.8 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), creatinine 62 micromol/L (45-90), serum osmolality 240 mOsm/kg (275-295), urine osmolality 380 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 42 mmol/L

lead_in: Given her symptoms, what is the most appropriate rate ceiling for correction of her serum sodium over the first 24 hours?

options.text: Correction should not exceed 8 mmol/L in the first 24 hours (with 6 mmol/L preferred in high-risk patients), after an initial 100 mL 3 percent saline bolus for symptomatic hyponatraemia
Correction may safely proceed at 15 mmol/L in the first 24 hours if the patient has severe neurological symptoms, using continuous 3 percent hypertonic saline infusion
Correction should aim for a return to normal sodium (135 mmol/L) within 12 hours of admission, as the confusion and drowsiness indicate impending herniation and immediate normalisation is life-saving
Correction should be limited to 4 mmol/L in the first 24 hours because the patient is asymptomatic and there is no urgency to correct the sodium in this setting
Correction should proceed at 12 mmol/L in the first 24 hours because the risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome only becomes significant beyond that rate of correction in a healthy adult

subtopic_detail: Type A aortic dissection with hypertension and stroke
stem:
A 64-year-old man presents to a metropolitan emergency department with sudden onset tearing central chest pain radiating to the back that began 90 minutes ago while shovelling in his garden. He has hypertension treated with amlodipine 5 mg daily and hyperlipidaemia treated with atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. He is now hemodynamically stable but continues to describe severe pain.

On arrival his right arm blood pressure is 176/98 and his left arm blood pressure is 128/72. His radial pulses are asymmetric. Neurological examination reveals right-sided hemiparesis (arm and leg 3 out of 5) and expressive dysphasia that began after arrival. A CT aortogram completed 15 minutes ago demonstrates a Stanford Type A dissection extending from the aortic root through the arch and involving the innominate artery, with a moderate pericardial effusion but no cardiac tamponade. Cardiothoracic surgery has been contacted.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 96, blood pressure 176/98 right arm and 128/72 left arm, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 138 g/L (130-180), platelets 240 x10 to the 9 per litre (150-400), troponin I 0.02 microgram/L (less than 0.03), creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110), ECG with sinus rhythm and no acute ischaemic changes
data_table.Imaging: CT aortogram with Stanford Type A dissection root through arch, innominate artery involved, moderate pericardial effusion without tamponade

lead_in: In addition to arranging emergency cardiothoracic transfer, what is the most appropriate initial medical management?

options.text: Commence intravenous alteplase 0.9 mg/kg for the acute ischaemic stroke, aiming to complete infusion within 60 minutes of stroke onset to salvage the penumbra
Administer intravenous esmolol infusion titrated to target heart rate under 60 with intravenous glyceryl trinitrate for target systolic under 120 in the higher-reading arm, and analgesia
Administer intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion alone without a rate-limiting beta blocker to rapidly reduce systolic blood pressure to under 120 mmHg
Administer subcutaneous enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily for suspected pulmonary embolism prophylaxis pending completion of CT pulmonary angiogram results
Perform urgent pericardiocentesis for the moderate pericardial effusion demonstrated on the CT aortogram before any medical or surgical intervention is undertaken

subtopic_detail: Necrotising soft tissue infection despite borderline LRINEC
stem:
A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin presents with a 24-hour history of severe left lower leg pain following a minor gardening scratch 3 days ago. The pain is disproportionate to the visible skin findings, which show a 6 cm area of erythema with poorly demarcated edges and a small area of dusky violaceous discolouration in the centre. There is subcutaneous crepitus on palpation of the medial calf. He appears systemically unwell with a temperature of 38.6 degrees and rigors.

His white cell count is 16 x10 to the 9 per litre, C-reactive protein 180 mg/L, sodium 136 mmol/L, creatinine 108 micromol/L, glucose 12 mmol/L (previous HbA1c 8.4 percent), and haemoglobin 138 g/L. His LRINEC score today is 6 (borderline: 6 to 7 indicates intermediate risk, 8 or above indicates high risk). Plain radiograph of the calf shows subcutaneous gas along the fascial planes. Blood cultures are pending.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 122, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 138 g/L (130-180), white cell count 16 x10 to the 9 per litre (4.0-11.0), CRP 180 mg/L (less than 5), sodium 136 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 108 micromol/L (60-110), glucose 12 mmol/L, LRINEC score 6
data_table.Imaging: plain radiograph left calf with subcutaneous gas along fascial planes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Await magnetic resonance imaging of the calf before proceeding to any operative intervention to define fascial involvement and target debridement extent precisely
Commence intravenous flucloxacillin monotherapy at 2 g every 6 hours for community-acquired cellulitis and mark the area of erythema for reassessment in 6 hours
Activate the emergency theatre pathway for urgent surgical exploration and debridement while starting empirical intravenous meropenem plus clindamycin and resuscitation
Repeat the LRINEC score in 6 hours and defer surgical exploration if the score remains below 8, using oral doxycycline for outpatient management in the meantime
Administer intravenous immunoglobulin as first-line empirical monotherapy for suspected streptococcal toxic shock syndrome and observe for haemodynamic response over 2 hours

stem:
A 52-year-old man with a history of intravenous methamphetamine use presents with three weeks of malaise, drenching night sweats and progressive dyspnoea. He describes cough with intermittent haemoptysis. He has never had rheumatic fever and had no known murmur previously.

He was febrile in triage. Transthoracic echocardiogram in ED shows a 12 mm mobile vegetation on the tricuspid valve with moderate tricuspid regurgitation. Three sets of peripheral blood cultures drawn 30 minutes apart are all positive for Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin sensitive).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 92 percent on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pansystolic murmur at left lower sternal edge increasing with inspiration; needle track marks in left cubital fossa; small vasculitic peripheral lesions
data_table.Investigations: Blood cultures 3 of 3 positive Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin sensitive); CRP 240 mg/L (below 5); WCC 18.4 x10^9/L; chest x-ray with bilateral peripheral cavitating nodules

lead_in: How does this case classify under the modified Duke criteria?

options.text: Rejected endocarditis pending transoesophageal echocardiography confirmation
Definite endocarditis by two major criteria; empirical benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin therapy
Possible endocarditis by one major and one minor criterion needing additional imaging
Definite endocarditis by one major and three minor criteria requiring valve replacement
Rejected endocarditis; treat as suspected pulmonary emboli with anticoagulation cover only

stem:
A 68-year-old man presents to ED with a two-day history of severe headache, vomiting and fever, brought in by his wife. He has been progressively drowsy over the last six hours. He is a heavy smoker with COPD and has diet-controlled type 2 diabetes.

On arrival his GCS is 12 (E3 V4 M5). He has neck stiffness and a positive Kernig's sign. He has no focal neurological deficit. His pupils are equal at 3 mm and briskly reactive. There is no petechial rash.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 95 percent on room air, temperature 39.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: GCS 12; neck stiffness; Kernig positive; no focal deficit; no papilloedema on fundoscopy; no petechiae
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.4 x10^9/L, CRP 340 mg/L (below 5); coags within normal limits; blood glucose 8.4 mmol/L; blood cultures taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment before lumbar puncture?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g and vancomycin 25 mg/kg targeting community meningitis pathogens
Intravenous benzylpenicillin 2.4 g and gentamicin 5 mg/kg empirically for suspected bacterial meningitis
Intravenous cefotaxime 2 g and metronidazole 500 mg targeting anaerobic and gram-negative cover
Intravenous dexamethasone 10 mg then ceftriaxone 2 g plus benzylpenicillin 2.4 g four hourly
Wait for lumbar puncture and CT brain results before starting empirical antibiotic therapy

subtopic_detail: Looking for a secondary cause before treating osteoporosis in a man
stem: A 58-year-old man fractures a rib lifting a box at work. Radiographs also show an old wedge fracture at T8. Bone densitometry shows a lumbar spine T-score of -3.0. He takes no regular medicines and has never used glucocorticoids.

data_table.Examination: Height 178 cm, BMI 24; no kyphosis; normal testicular examination
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.28 mmol/L; eGFR 84 mL/min; vitamin D 62 nmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Send testosterone, coeliac serology and protein electrophoresis
Start weekly oral alendronate now without any further investigation
Arrange a radionuclide bone scan of the whole skeleton first
Repeat bone densitometry in two years before starting any treatment
Refer for a transiliac bone biopsy with tetracycline labelling

stem:
A 72-year-old man presents from a nursing home with two days of increasing confusion, dysuria and fever. On arrival to ED he is peripherally cool with capillary refill of 4 seconds. He has diet-controlled type 2 diabetes and hypertension on perindopril.

After 30 mL/kg of intravenous crystalloid over 45 minutes his MAP is 58 mmHg and his lactate is 4.2 mmol/L (down from 5.1 on arrival). Urine dip shows leucocytes and nitrites. Blood cultures were drawn before piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g was started at the 30 minute mark. He has not passed urine in six hours.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 88/44 mmHg (MAP 58), respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 94 percent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert but drowsy, GCS 13; cool peripheries; capillary refill 4 seconds; soft abdomen with suprapubic tenderness; no rash
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.2 mmol/L post-resuscitation; blood cultures pending; WCC 22.4 x10^9/L; creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 92); potassium 4.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Give another 10 mL/kg crystalloid bolus and reassess in 15 minutes before starting vasopressor
Change perindopril to intravenous dihydralazine to improve renal perfusion
Start noradrenaline peripheral infusion via large vein while arranging central venous access
Give intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg per day continuous infusion for refractory septic shock
Change antibiotics to meropenem 1 g IV eight hourly for broader spectrum sepsis cover

stem:
A 34-year-old woman presents with a 48-hour history of vomiting, abdominal pain and progressive weakness. She has known Addison's disease diagnosed three years ago and takes hydrocortisone 10 mg morning, 5 mg afternoon and fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily. She has not been able to keep tablets down for 24 hours.

She reports a fever and cough for four days before the vomiting started. She is normally well and her most recent endocrinology review last month was unremarkable. She carries an emergency injection kit but has not used it.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 38.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but responsive; dry mucous membranes; hyperpigmented palmar creases; capillary refill 4 seconds; abdomen soft with generalised tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 128 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 5.8 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), glucose 3.4 mmol/L (below 4.0), urea 11.2 mmol/L; VBG pH 7.30, HCO3 18 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus and start 0.9 percent sodium chloride resuscitation
Wait for 09:00 cortisol result and Synacthen stimulation before hydrocortisone administration
Give intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg because it does not interfere with cortisol assay
Give intravenous insulin plus dextrose for the hyperkalaemia and delay steroid to after correction
Double her usual oral hydrocortisone dose today and admit for overnight observation

stem:
A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents with a 24-hour history of severe left thigh pain that started after a minor trampoline injury with his grandchildren. He describes the pain as out of proportion to what the skin looks like, and it has escalated from moderate to unbearable overnight. He looks unwell.

Examination shows a swollen left thigh with tenderness extending well beyond the erythematous area. There is dusky skin discolouration medially with two small bullae, and crepitus is palpable on the anterior thigh. The overlying skin is warm but not obviously fluctuant.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Left thigh with dusky discolouration medially, two small bullae, crepitus anteriorly; pain out of proportion to visual signs; peripheral pulses present
data_table.Investigations: CRP 320 mg/L (below 5); WCC 24.6 x10^9/L; sodium 133 mmol/L; creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 88); glucose 14.8 mmol/L; haemoglobin 108 g/L (130 to 180); LRINEC score 11

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g four hourly and mark erythema border for 6 hourly review
Emergency surgical debridement with concurrent broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy as monotherapy before considering surgical debridement
Bedside incision and drainage under local anaesthetic in the emergency department
Wait for MRI imaging with gadolinium confirmation before proceeding to theatre for surgery

stem:
An 82-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin only is brought in by his son with two weeks of increasing confusion. He has drunk less than usual because he lives alone and thinks his son forgot to bring water. He has no chest pain or focal deficit but is very drowsy on arrival.

His capillary glucose meter reads high (above 33). Formal glucose is 62 mmol/L. His son reports no polyuria historically. He has not vomited and has no abdominal pain. He was independent in his own home four weeks ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: GCS 12; dry mucous membranes; tenting skin turgor; no ketotic breath; abdomen soft; no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 62 mmol/L, ketones 0.9 mmol/L, sodium 156 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, urea 28 mmol/L, creatinine 220 micromol/L, VBG pH 7.32, HCO3 20 mmol/L, calculated osmolality 380 mOsm/kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid strategy?

options.text: Intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride 500 mL bolus and start insulin 0.1 units/kg/hour immediately
Intravenous Hartmann's 20 mL/kg bolus then insulin 0.05 units/kg/hour after 2 hours
Intravenous 0.45 percent sodium chloride at 250 mL per hour without any insulin therapy
Intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride 250 mL bolus then 5 percent dextrose infusion at 100 mL/hour
Intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride 1 litre over 1 hour then reassess before starting insulin

stem:
A 32-year-old woman is brought to a regional ED after a high-speed motor vehicle collision. She has a distended abdomen with generalised tenderness and a suspected pelvic fracture on FAST-positive imaging. She has already received 1 litre of 0.9 percent sodium chloride and 1 unit of O negative packed red cells.

Her initial haemoglobin was 82 g/L (115 to 165) and lactate 5.4 mmol/L. Her INR just returned at 1.8. The retrieval team is 45 minutes away. She has just received 4 units of packed red cells across the last 20 minutes and is still bleeding actively.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138/min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 30/min, SpO2 96 percent on 15 L non-rebreather, temperature 35.1 degrees C
data_table.Examination: GCS 13; pelvic binder in place; distended tender abdomen; peripheral cool with capillary refill 5 seconds; ongoing large-volume bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 82 g/L; INR 1.8; platelet 108 x10^9/L; fibrinogen 1.6 g/L (2.0 to 4.0); ionised calcium 1.02 mmol/L (1.15 to 1.30); lactate 5.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate combined next management step?

options.text: Continue packed red cells only until INR corrects below 1.5 before adding fresh frozen plasma
Give intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g only and continue packed red cells as the next step
Give warm crystalloid 2 litres and elevate legs to increase preload before further blood products
Activate MTP with RBC to FFP to platelets 1:1:1, tranexamic acid 1 g, cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen
Give prothrombin complex concentrate 25 units/kg to correct INR before further transfusion

subtopic_detail: Right-sided endocarditis in an IV drug user
stem:
A 32-year-old man with a history of intravenous heroin use presents with 5 days of fevers to 39.5 degrees, rigors, and a dry cough with mild pleuritic chest pain. He last injected 8 days ago. On examination he is warm and diaphoretic with tender needle-track marks in the left antecubital fossa. Chest auscultation is clear. Cardiac auscultation reveals a soft systolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge that varies with respiration.

He is hepatitis C positive and untreated, HIV negative on testing 6 months ago. Chest X-ray shows scattered bilateral peripheral rounded infiltrates. Blood cultures have been drawn from two separate sites.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112/min, blood pressure 106/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 94 percent on room air, temperature 39.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert; needle-track marks left antecubital fossa; soft tricuspid systolic murmur that varies with respiration; chest clear
data_table.Investigations: WCC 16.4 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 210 mg/L (<5); troponin within normal limits; chest X-ray: bilateral peripheral rounded infiltrates; ECG sinus tachycardia; blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 hours plus vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose
Intravenous benzylpenicillin 2.4 g every 4 hours plus gentamicin 4 to 5 mg/kg daily
Oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily plus rifampicin as outpatient management now
Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 6 hours plus gentamicin daily
Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily as monotherapy pending culture and echocardiography

stem:
A 26-year-old man attends a sexual health clinic 12 days after a condomless receptive anal sex encounter with a new partner of unknown HIV status. He has had a febrile illness for 4 days with pharyngitis, myalgias, headache and a fine truncal maculopapular rash. He denies genital ulcers. A rapid fourth-generation antibody-antigen combination assay in-clinic is negative. He has never previously been tested for HIV and has not taken PEP.

He has no significant medical history, is on no regular medications, and is otherwise well. He has already agreed to further testing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Fine truncal maculopapular rash; pharyngeal erythema without exudate; bilateral non-tender cervical lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Fourth-generation HIV Ab-Ag combined assay negative; syphilis serology, hepatitis B/C serology, gonorrhoea and chlamydia PCR sent; monospot pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?

options.text: Repeat the fourth-generation antibody-antigen assay in 8 weeks after exposure
Order HIV Western blot confirmatory testing on the same sample tomorrow morning
Order CD4 lymphocyte subset counts to look for a fall consistent with primary infection
Test for Epstein-Barr virus IgM antibody as most likely alternative cause of the rash
Order HIV RNA (viral load) PCR now for detection during the antibody window period

A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents with 24 hours of a red, swollen and exquisitely tender left lower leg after a minor gardening abrasion. Pain is severe and out of proportion to visible skin changes. There are patches of dusky discolouration in the calf and small tense bullae are developing. He has generalised systemic symptoms with rigors.

He last used insulin 8 hours ago. He has no known allergies. Bloods were drawn on arrival and IV access is established.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Left calf red, hot, swollen with dusky patches and small tense bullae; exquisite tenderness; sensation reduced over lateral calf; distal pulses palpable
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.8 x10^9/L (4-11), Hb 118 g/L (135-175), sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), glucose 14.2 mmol/L, creatinine 168 micromol/L (60-110), CRP 342 mg/L (<5), lactate 4.6 mmol/L; LRINEC score 8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Elevate the leg and start oral flucloxacillin 500 mg 6-hourly with community follow-up
Immediate surgical review for urgent debridement plus broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
MRI leg with contrast to confirm fascial involvement before considering surgical review
IV vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose alone with ward observation and hourly review
Skin punch biopsy at the affected calf site for Gram stain and culture before treatment

A 42-year-old woman with known Addison's disease is brought to ED by her partner with 24 hours of vomiting, abdominal pain and increasing lethargy after a gastroenteritis illness. She takes hydrocortisone 20 mg on waking, 5 mg at midday and 5 mg at 4pm, plus fludrocortisone 100 microgram daily. She has been unable to keep down her morning hydrocortisone dose today. She is drowsy but rousable, feels dizzy on sitting, and looks pigmented.

Her partner reports that she did not double her hydrocortisone dose despite the illness. There is no fever and no localising infective source.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122/min supine, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg supine, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but oriented; hyperpigmented palmar creases; dry mucous membranes; abdomen soft with mild diffuse tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), creatinine 132 micromol/L (60-110); venous gas pH 7.28, HCO3 14 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 50 mg with intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride at 250 mL/hour
Increase fludrocortisone to 200 microgram orally and give oral rehydration solution
IV dexamethasone 4 mg with intravenous fluid resuscitation and glucose supplementation
IV noradrenaline infusion to restore blood pressure before hydrocortisone administration
IV hydrocortisone 100 mg then 200 mg over 24 hours with intravenous fluid resuscitation

stem:
A 44-year-old man presents to ED with 5 days of ascending symmetric limb weakness that started with distal paraesthesia in the feet. He is now unable to walk unaided and has weakness in his shoulder girdle. He had gastroenteritis 3 weeks ago. His forced vital capacity at the bedside is 22 mL/kg (predicted 60 mL/kg). Reflexes are absent at the ankles and knees and reduced in the upper limbs.

Swallow is intact at bedside review. Cranial nerve examination is normal apart from a mild bilateral facial weakness. He has no bladder or bowel dysfunction.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Symmetric flaccid limb weakness power 3/5 lower limbs, 4/5 upper limbs; absent lower limb and reduced upper limb reflexes; bilateral facial weakness; sensation reduced to pinprick distally
data_table.Investigations: CSF: protein 0.98 g/L (0.15-0.45), WCC 3/mm3, glucose within normal limits; nerve conduction studies show reduced motor amplitudes with prolonged distal latencies; FVC 22 mL/kg predicted 60

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immunotherapy?

options.text: Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days followed by oral prednisolone
Intravenous immunoglobulin 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days with respiratory monitoring
Combined IVIG and plasma exchange sequentially over 2 weeks with steroid cover
Oral azathioprine 2 mg/kg daily with weekly IVIG boosters for 3 to 6 months
Supportive care alone with high dependency unit observation and physiotherapy support

A 46-year-old woman presents to rheumatology outpatients with 10 weeks of symmetric small joint pain and morning stiffness lasting 90 minutes. On examination there is tender synovitis in 8 metacarpophalangeal joints and both wrists. Rheumatoid factor is positive at 108 IU/mL and anti-CCP is positive at over 200 U/mL. CRP is elevated at 52 mg/L. She has no significant medical history and does not drink alcohol.

Hand X-rays are normal without erosions. She has no plans for pregnancy and is currently using an intrauterine device. She has no active infection.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Bilateral symmetric MCP and wrist synovitis; DAS28 5.4; no rheumatoid nodules; no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: RF 108 IU/mL (<15), anti-CCP over 200 U/mL, CRP 52 mg/L (<5), ESR 68 mm/hr; LFTs, U and E, hepatitis B/C, TB QuantiFERON, chest X-ray all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial DMARD?

options.text: Sulfasalazine 500 mg twice daily titrating slowly to 2 g daily over 4 weeks
Hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily as sole disease-modifying therapy at start
Adalimumab 40 mg subcutaneous every 2 weeks as first-line biologic monotherapy now
Methotrexate 15 mg orally once weekly with folic acid 5 mg once weekly the next day
Oral prednisolone 30 mg daily long-term as monotherapy until disease remission achieved

An 82-year-old woman on warfarin for atrial fibrillation presents by ambulance with a 6-hour history of confusion, right-sided weakness and headache after a fall. CT brain shows a 25 mL left frontoparietal intraparenchymal haemorrhage with 3 mm midline shift. Her INR on arrival is 4.2. Her weight is 68 kg. She is drowsy but rousable with a Glasgow Coma Score of 12.

She takes no other anticoagulant, has stable renal function and no known allergies to vitamin K or blood products. Neurosurgery has been contacted.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 172/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5); right-sided facial droop and 3/5 weakness in the right arm; pupils equal and reactive; no meningism
data_table.Investigations: INR 4.2 (target 2-3); creatinine 82 micromol/L (60-110); platelets 240 x10^9/L; CT: 25 mL left frontoparietal intraparenchymal haemorrhage with 3 mm midline shift

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reversal strategy?

options.text: Vitamin K 10 mg orally with fresh frozen plasma 4 units and 6-hourly INR checks
Fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg without vitamin K and repeat INR after 4 hours
Idarucizumab 5 g intravenously with intravenous vitamin K 10 mg co-administered
Recombinant activated factor VII 40 microgram/kg with vitamin K 10 mg intravenously
Prothrombinex-VF 50 IU/kg intravenously plus vitamin K 5 to 10 mg intravenously

A 58-year-old man had a proximal right femoral vein deep vein thrombosis 6 months ago with no identifiable provoking factor. He has been on apixaban 5 mg twice daily since diagnosis and has had no bleeding complications. Follow-up screening for cancer was negative, and thrombophilia screening was negative. He is well and asymptomatic today.

His HAS-BLED score is 1 (age over 65 not yet reached). Blood pressure is controlled and there is no history of GI bleeding, renal impairment or falls. He is fit and physically active.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Well; no calf swelling or tenderness; no bruising; no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: FBC and U and E within normal limits; creatinine clearance 82 mL/min; ferritin, iron studies and faecal occult blood negative; imaging follow-up 6 months post-DVT unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate long-term anticoagulation plan?

options.text: Stop anticoagulation today as the initial 6-month treatment course is now complete
Reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg twice daily indefinitely for continued VTE prevention
Continue indefinite anticoagulation; reduced-dose apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily is preferred
Switch to aspirin 100 mg daily indefinitely as extended prevention with lower bleeding risk
Switch to warfarin with target INR 2 to 3 and cease DOAC use going forward

stem:
A 68-year-old man presents with 3 months of nasal crusting, epistaxis, purpuric rash on the lower limbs and a 7 kg weight loss. He now has haemoptysis over the past week and shortness of breath on stairs. Creatinine has risen from 88 micromol/L six months ago to 262 micromol/L today. Urinalysis shows haematuria and proteinuria with red cell casts on microscopy. Chest CT shows patchy bilateral cavitating pulmonary nodules.

He has no active infection on screening. Hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, QuantiFERON and beta-D-glucan are negative. Kidney biopsy has been arranged.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 152/90 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 95 percent on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Purpuric palpable lesions on lower limbs; nasal crusting with a septal defect; chest with scattered coarse crackles bibasally
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 262 micromol/L (60-110), urine PCR 320 mg/mmol; c-ANCA positive with PR3 titre elevated; kidney biopsy pending; chest CT bilateral cavitating nodules; complement C3 and C4 within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate induction therapy?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 60 mg daily as monotherapy with hydroxychloroquine and calcium
Intravenous rituximab 375 mg/m2 weekly for 4 weeks plus glucocorticoid taper
Plasma exchange every second day for 14 days as sole induction without steroid cover
Oral cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg daily for 3 months with folate and steroid support
Methotrexate 15 mg weekly with folate and low-dose prednisolone as sole induction

stem: A 74-year-old woman taking weekly alendronate for six years describes six weeks of aching in the right groin and thigh, worse on walking and now present at rest. She has had no fall. Hip movements are full and pain free.

data_table.Examination: Antalgic gait; tenderness over the lateral right thigh; no shortening or rotation
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.30 mmol/L; vitamin D 70 nmol/L; eGFR 72 mL/min

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Radiograph both femurs and withhold the alendronate meanwhile
Continue alendronate and refer for hip and knee physiotherapy
Arrange a lumbar spine radiograph looking for a nerve root cause
Switch to subcutaneous denosumab and review her in six months
Start regular paracetamol and review again in eight weeks' time

A 54-year-old man presents to your practice for review 3 months after his first episode of unprovoked proximal DVT of the right femoral vein. He has completed 3 months of therapeutic apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily and is asymptomatic. He is a lifelong non-smoker with no active malignancy, no recent surgery, no travel and no hormonal therapy.

His only medication is amlodipine 5 mg for essential hypertension. He walks the dog daily and works as an office manager. His HAS-BLED score is 1 (hypertension only). He is anxious about recurrence and asks whether he should continue anticoagulation indefinitely. Baseline thrombophilia screen was not performed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Right calf soft, no residual swelling; no signs of chronic venous insufficiency; no chest signs
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs within normal limits; D-dimer today not yet measured; HAS-BLED score 1

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan?

options.text: Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily indefinitely with annual bleeding-risk reassessment
Stop apixaban immediately and switch to warfarin with a target INR of 2.0 to 3.0
Cease apixaban now and start daily aspirin 100 mg as long-term secondary prevention only
Reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg twice daily as extended prophylaxis with periodic review
Cease all anticoagulation and use graduated compression stockings for prophylaxis only

A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman is reviewed after sustaining a minimal trauma right distal radius fracture after tripping on a footpath 6 weeks ago. DXA at L1-L4 shows a T-score of -3.1 and femoral neck T-score of -2.8. She has no prior fragility fractures and no known secondary causes of osteoporosis. Her serum calcium is 2.32 mmol/L, 25-OH vitamin D is 78 nmol/L, and TSH is within normal limits.

Her creatinine clearance is 62 mL/min. She has no dental problems and has not had any dental extractions or oral surgery planned. She lives independently and has no history of falls in the last 12 months apart from this one. Her calcium intake is 800 mg per day from diet.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Right wrist in a cast with adequate function; no other joint tenderness; no kyphosis clinically
data_table.Investigations: DXA L1-L4 T-score -3.1, femoral neck -2.8; corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.10-2.60); 25-OH vitamin D 78 nmol/L; creatinine clearance 62 mL/min; TSH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Strontium ranelate 2 g daily as first-line antiresorptive plus anabolic combined therapy
Subcutaneous denosumab 60 mg every 6 months as immediate first-line therapy without any bisphosphonate trial
Teriparatide 20 microgram subcutaneously daily for the first 18 months of therapy
Continuous combined menopausal hormone therapy as monotherapy for osteoporosis prevention
Oral alendronate 70 mg once weekly with adequate calcium and vitamin D intake maintained

stem:
An 82-year-old man is reviewed in your practice after his third fall in 6 months. All falls have been at home, without loss of consciousness, and one resulted in a Colles fracture. He lives with his wife and mobilises with a 4-wheeled walker. His medications include amitriptyline 25 mg nocte for chronic low back pain, temazepam 10 mg nocte for insomnia, oxybutynin 5 mg BD for urge incontinence, perindopril 5 mg mane, metformin 1 g BD, and rosuvastatin 20 mg nocte.

He denies angina, syncope or palpitations. Postural BP shows a drop from 138/82 lying to 108/68 standing after 3 minutes with a corresponding 12 bpm heart rate rise. Cognition is intact (MoCA 27/30). Timed Up and Go is 22 seconds. Vision is normal with current glasses.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, lying blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, standing blood pressure 108/68 mmHg at 3 minutes, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, oriented, MoCA 27/30, TUG 22 seconds; power 4+/5 lower limbs bilaterally with normal reflexes and normal joint position sense
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, TSH, B12 all within normal limits; ECG sinus rhythm at 72; HbA1c 6.9 percent

lead_in: Which medication change should be the immediate priority?

options.text: Cease temazepam and amitriptyline with a plan to review analgesic strategy separately
Reduce perindopril to 2.5 mg daily to address postural blood pressure change immediately
Cease rosuvastatin 20 mg to remove any risk of statin-associated myopathy contributing here
Stop metformin because of the small risk of unrecognised hypoglycaemia in an older man
Increase oxybutynin to 10 mg TDS to reduce nocturia and thus night-time toileting falls

A 32-year-old man is diagnosed with HIV after a routine STI screen prompted by high-risk sexual practices. His baseline CD4 count is 480 cells/microlitre, HIV RNA viral load is 82,000 copies/mL, and HLA-B*5701 is negative. Confirmatory Western blot is positive. He has no opportunistic infections and is otherwise well. Baseline biochemistry, hepatitis serology (HBV surface antigen negative, immune to HAV, HCV negative) and syphilis serology are unremarkable.

He is highly motivated for treatment and asks about starting antiretroviral therapy at his next visit. He works full-time in hospitality and has good private health insurance. He has no active psychiatric symptoms and is not injecting drugs.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert; no lymphadenopathy; no oral candida; no rashes; chest clear; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: CD4 480 cells/microlitre; HIV RNA 82,000 copies/mL; HLA-B*5701 negative; HBsAg negative; HAV IgG positive; HCV negative; creatinine 78 micromol/L; ALT 26 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antiretroviral plan?

options.text: Defer therapy until CD4 falls below 350 cells/microlitre before commencing combination therapy
Commence a single-tablet regimen of bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide within days
Start efavirenz-based combination therapy at initial diagnosis because of cost advantage
Commence dolutegravir monotherapy while awaiting resistance testing and full staging results
Prescribe abacavir plus lamivudine plus dolutegravir triple therapy without HLA typing

A 28-year-old woman from Vietnam has been in Australia for 12 months. She is a nurse and completed pre-employment screening. Her interferon-gamma release assay (QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus) returned positive. She has no cough, night sweats, weight loss or fevers. Chest X-ray is clear. She has no history of BCG vaccination that she can recall.

She is HIV negative and not immunosuppressed. She is on the combined oral contraceptive pill. LFTs are within normal limits. She has no personal or family history of liver disease and drinks no alcohol. She is not pregnant and does not plan to conceive in the next year. She is highly motivated to complete treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert; no lymphadenopathy; chest clear on auscultation; abdomen soft with no hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus positive; chest X-ray clear; HIV negative; ALT 22 U/L (<40); ALT normal; bilirubin normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment regimen?

options.text: Rifampicin 600 mg daily monotherapy for 4 months without concurrent isoniazid cover
Isoniazid 300 mg daily plus rifampicin 600 mg daily for 12 months orally at home
Isoniazid 300 mg daily plus rifapentine weekly for 12 weeks under directly observed therapy
Directly observed active TB treatment with 4 drugs regardless of chest X-ray result
Observation with annual QuantiFERON testing and no pharmacotherapy for the latent infection

Hand X-rays are unremarkable for erosions but show soft tissue swelling around the MCPs.

She has completed her family and is not breastfeeding. She drinks no alcohol. LFTs and renal function are within normal limits. She is up to date with cervical screening. Chest X-ray is clear. Rheumatology outpatient wait time is 6 weeks. She is otherwise well.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Symmetric synovitis of MCP 2-4 and PIP 2-4 bilaterally with soft swelling; power maintained; no rheumatoid nodules
data_table.Investigations: Rheumatoid factor 68 IU/mL; anti-CCP 108 U/mL; CRP 48 mg/L; ESR 62 mm/hr; ALT 22 U/L; creatinine 68 micromol/L; hand X-rays: soft tissue swelling only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Refer to rheumatology in 6 weeks and give no medical management pending specialist input
Prescribe oral prednisolone 20 mg daily and defer any DMARD selection to specialist review
Prescribe naproxen 500 mg twice daily and celecoxib 200 mg for symptom control only
Commence oral methotrexate 15 mg weekly with folic acid 5 mg weekly and urgent rheumatology referral
Immediate high-dose infliximab infusion in the community without prior methotrexate trial

stem:
A 32-year-old woman presents to your practice with 6 migraine episodes per month over the past 4 months. Each episode lasts 24 hours, causes her to miss work, and responds partially to oral sumatriptan 50 mg. She has no aura. Her past medical history includes moderate persistent asthma well-controlled on Symbicort maintenance and reliever. She has no depression, no cardiac history, and no pregnancy plans over the next 12 months.

Her only regular medications are Symbicort and paracetamol as needed. She does not use oral contraception. She has trialled magnesium 400 mg daily for 3 months without benefit. She has identified triggers of poor sleep and skipping meals which she is addressing with sleep hygiene and structured eating.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, oriented; cranial nerve exam within normal limits; no focal neurology; fundi normal
data_table.Investigations: FBC, TSH, UEC within normal limits; no imaging indicated by red flag review

lead_in: What is the most appropriate migraine prophylaxis to commence?

options.text: Propranolol 40 mg twice daily titrated to 80 mg twice daily over 4 weeks as needed
Continue current sumatriptan and add regular paracetamol daily as prophylaxis at home
Sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily titrated to 1500 mg total daily dose over 4 weeks
Verapamil 80 mg three times daily as prophylaxis with cardiac ECG at baseline before start
Amitriptyline 10 mg nocte titrated up to 25 to 50 mg nocte over 4 to 6 weeks as tolerated

stem:
A 42-year-old woman presents to your practice with 12 months of progressive central weight gain (9 kg), easy bruising on her arms with minimal trauma, new-onset hypertension requiring a second agent, oligomenorrhoea and mood lability. Her mother had breast cancer at 62. She has striae 8 mm wide across her abdomen and flanks that are purple. She takes amlodipine 5 mg and irbesartan 150 mg for blood pressure.

She has no exogenous glucocorticoid use, including no inhaled or intra-articular steroids. She drinks 1 to 2 standard drinks per week and does not shift-work. Random morning cortisol taken by another practitioner was 480 nmol/L. Fasting glucose is 6.8 mmol/L, and HbA1c is 6.5 percent.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 158/94 mmHg on two agents, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Central adiposity with dorsocervical fat pad; wide purple striae on abdomen and flanks; proximal muscle weakness; easy bruising on arms
data_table.Investigations: Random morning cortisol 480 nmol/L; fasting glucose 6.8 mmol/L; HbA1c 6.5 percent; potassium 3.6 mmol/L; no exogenous steroid use

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line screening investigation?

options.text: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test with morning cortisol at 08:00 the next day
Plasma ACTH measurement in a single early morning sample as the initial screening test
Inferior petrosal sinus sampling to localise the source of ACTH secretion definitively
Random single serum cortisol interpreted against a fixed cut-off value of 500 nanomole/L
CT of the adrenal glands and pituitary MRI before any biochemical confirmation is undertaken

stem:
A 68-year-old male ex-smoker (30 pack-years, quit 8 years ago) presents to your respiratory outpatient clinic with 12 months of progressive exertional dyspnoea and a dry cough. He has bibasal fine end-inspiratory crackles and finger clubbing. His FVC is 68 percent predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.85, and DLCO is 42 percent predicted.

He has no rash, joint symptoms, or Raynaud's phenomenon. Autoimmune serology (ANA, ENA, anti-CCP, RF, MPO, PR3) is negative. He has never worked in mining, construction or with asbestos. HRCT chest today shows peripheral and basal reticulation with honeycombing 5 mm subpleural cysts and traction bronchiectasis, with no ground glass and no mediastinal lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 94 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C

data_table.Investigations: Spirometry: FVC 68 percent predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.85, DLCO 42 percent predicted; autoimmune serology negative; HRCT: definite UIP pattern with honeycombing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Empirical high-dose prednisolone 60 mg daily for 6 weeks to arrest disease progression
Refer to a specialist ILD multidisciplinary team for antifibrotic therapy consideration
Surgical lung biopsy from the right lower lobe to obtain definitive tissue diagnosis first
N-acetylcysteine 600 mg three times daily as antioxidant monotherapy for slow progression
Reassurance and 12-month observation with repeat HRCT to confirm progression before treatment

stem:
