He usually lives independently and manages his own affairs but today he cannot recall the day of the week. He has stage 3 CKD (baseline creatinine 150 micromol/L) and hypertension.

On examination he has bronchial breathing at the left lower zone and dullness to percussion. Chest X-ray shows left lower lobe consolidation. SMART-COP score is 5. His lactate is 3.4 mmol/L, WCC 22 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 240 mg/L. Blood cultures have been taken. He is not immunosuppressed and has no known drug allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 89 percent on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: New confusion (AMT 6/10); bronchial breathing left lower zone with dullness to percussion; peripheries cool
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22 x10^9/L (4-11); CRP 240 mg/L; lactate 3.4 mmol/L; creatinine 220 micromol/L; blood cultures pending; CXR left lower lobe consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic combination?

options.text: IV amoxicillin 1 g plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg and oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily now
Oral amoxicillin 1 g plus oral doxycycline 100 mg for community treatment at home tonight
IV ceftriaxone 1 g plus IV azithromycin 500 mg then IV fluid resuscitation and reassessment
IV piperacillin/tazobactam 4.5 g plus IV vancomycin as broad-spectrum first-line therapy
IV meropenem 1 g monotherapy every 8 hours for empirical broad-spectrum antimicrobial cover

stem:
A 34-year-old woman presents to your general practice with 24 hours of fever, right flank pain, dysuria and urinary frequency. She has vomited once but tolerates oral fluids and food now. She has no relevant past medical history and takes no regular medications. She is not pregnant (recent period 10 days ago, contraception with the LNG-IUS in situ).

On examination she has right renal angle tenderness and mild suprapubic tenderness without peritonism. Urinalysis shows blood, leucocytes and nitrites; MSU sent. She has social supports at home and can attend for reassessment at 48 hours if needed. She is not systemically septic - HR 92, BP 122/76, RR 18, SpO2 99, temperature 38.4.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert; abdomen soft with right renal angle tenderness and mild suprapubic tenderness; no peritonism; genitalia unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick: blood, leucocytes and nitrites; MSU sent; not pregnant

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days at home with a review at 48 hours in clinic
Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg four times daily for 7 days from your general practice today
Admit for IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg and IV ampicillin every 6 hours until afebrile 48 hours
Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 7 days with clinic review at 48 hours from now
Oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days as first-line empirical antibiotic therapy

stem:
A 74-year-old woman on warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve replacement (target INR 2.5 to 3.5) presents to the emergency department with a 4-hour history of sudden severe headache and left-sided weakness. Her CT brain shows a right-sided intracerebral haemorrhage in the basal ganglia measuring 35 mm with mild midline shift. Her INR on arrival is 3.8.

She is drowsy but rousable, moving all four limbs with 3/5 power on the left and 5/5 on the right. She was last stable INR 3 weeks ago at 2.6. Her regular medications also include perindopril, amlodipine and atorvastatin. She has no known drug allergies. She weighs 68 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 176/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: GCS 13 (E3V4M6); left hemiparesis 3/5; right side 5/5; pupils equal and reactive
data_table.Investigations: INR 3.8; APTT 42 sec; platelets 210 x10^9/L (150-450); creatinine 92 micromol/L; CT brain: 35 mm right basal ganglia ICH with mild midline shift

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate reversal strategy?

options.text: Recombinant activated factor VII (rFVIIa) as a single bolus dose given intravenously today
Vitamin K 10 mg oral only and observe INR trend for the next 6 hours prior to reassessment
Fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg IV alone as reversal without any additional intervention
Idarucizumab 5 g IV as immediate warfarin reversal in the emergency department resuscitation
Vitamin K 10 mg IV plus prothrombinex 50 units/kg IV given as soon as they can be prepared

subtopic_detail: HIV opportunistic infection prophylaxis by CD4 count
stem:
A 38-year-old man newly diagnosed with HIV attends your general practice for co-management with the ID physician. His baseline bloods show HIV viral load 240000 copies/mL, CD4 count 140 cells/microL, and toxoplasma IgG negative. He is asymptomatic and antiretroviral therapy (bictegravir/tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine) is being started this week. His BMI is 24 kg/m2, blood pressure is normal.

He has no allergies. His previous investigations show normal renal function, LFTs and glucose. Latent tuberculosis screening with QFT-Plus is pending and CXR was clear. He is up to date with all vaccinations and has already received the annual influenza vaccine.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No lymphadenopathy; no oral candidiasis; chest clear; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: HIV VL 240000 copies/mL; CD4 140 cells/microL; toxoplasma IgG negative; QFT-Plus pending; CXR clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate prophylaxis regimen to commence now?

options.text: Fluconazole 200 mg orally daily for oesophageal candida and cryptococcal prophylaxis today
Ganciclovir 1 g orally three times daily for CMV retinitis prophylaxis regardless of CMV status
Dapsone 100 mg orally daily plus pyrimethamine-folinic acid today as combined regimen
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg orally daily as sole opportunistic infection prophylaxis for now
Azithromycin 1200 mg orally weekly for Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis today

subtopic_detail: Osteoporosis pharmacological threshold from DXA and FRAX
stem:
A 66-year-old woman presents to your general practice for a routine health check. She is postmenopausal since age 52 and has never used menopausal hormone therapy. Her mother had a hip fracture at age 78. She takes calcium 500 mg daily and vitamin D 1000 IU daily. She has never had a fragility fracture herself, but she stumbled twice in the last year without injury.

Her BMI is 24 kg/m2, blood pressure normal, and she does not smoke or drink alcohol. Recent DXA scan reports lumbar spine T-score of -2.6, femoral neck T-score of -2.7 and total hip T-score of -2.4. Her calculated 10-year FRAX for major osteoporotic fracture is 22 percent and 10-year hip fracture risk is 5.2 percent.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No kyphosis; no bony tenderness; mobility unaided; no gait abnormality
data_table.Investigations: DXA lumbar spine T -2.6; femoral neck T -2.7; total hip T -2.4; 10-year FRAX major osteoporotic 22 percent; hip 5.2 percent; corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.15-2.60); vitamin D 78 nmol/L (>=50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological plan?

options.text: Repeat DXA scan in 2 years without any change to current calcium and vitamin D regimen
Start teriparatide 20 microgram subcutaneous daily as first-line treatment straightaway
Commence tibolone 2.5 mg daily for combined osteoporosis and vasomotor symptom management
Start strontium ranelate 2 g daily instead of a bisphosphonate for equivalent fracture prevention
Commence oral alendronate 70 mg weekly with continued calcium and vitamin D supplementation

stem:
A 54-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 6 hour severe frontal headache, blurred vision, and one episode of vomiting. She has a background of hypertension on ramipril 10 mg daily but has been non-adherent for 3 weeks. She does not smoke. On arrival her BP is 218/128 mmHg confirmed on repeat measurement, pulse 96/min sinus. Neurological examination shows no focal deficit but grade 3 hypertensive retinopathy with flame haemorrhages bilaterally on fundoscopy.

Her creatinine is 138 micromol/L (compared to 88 baseline 6 months ago), urinalysis shows 2+ protein and no red cells, troponin is negative and ECG shows LV hypertrophy without ST changes. CT brain is unremarkable and demonstrates no haemorrhage. She has no chest pain and no aortic dissection features.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 218/128 mmHg (repeated), respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: GCS 15; no focal neurology; grade 3 retinopathy with flame haemorrhages; chest clear; no cardiac murmur
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 138 micromol/L (baseline 88); urinalysis 2+ protein; troponin negative; ECG LVH; CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial antihypertensive?

options.text: IV labetalol 20 mg bolus with a target BP reduction of 25 percent over the first hour then further gradual reduction
IV nitroprusside starting at 3 microgram/kg/min targeting BP of 120/80 within 30 minutes
Sublingual nifedipine 20 mg immediate-release for rapid uncontrolled reduction as the sole intervention
Resume oral ramipril 10 mg once daily with observation over 4 hours as sole intervention
IV thiazide diuretic bolus of furosemide 40 mg alone as monotherapy for acute BP control

stem:
A 59-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin and empagliflozin presents to the emergency department with severe pain and swelling of his right leg for 24 hours. The pain seems disproportionate to the visible cellulitis on his shin. He described the affected area as feeling numb over the past 2 hours. He has crepitus on palpation and a small area of dusky discolouration. He has no recent trauma but reports a small unnoticed skin abrasion 3 days ago.

On examination he looks unwell, is confused (GCS 14), and has marked tenderness over the shin extending along the fascial planes. Blood tests: WCC 22 x10^9/L, Hb 128 g/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, creatinine 148 micromol/L, glucose 16 mmol/L, CRP 240 mg/L. Lactate 3.2 mmol/L. He is fluid-responsive but tachycardic.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122/min, blood pressure 96/62 mmHg (improved to 106 after 1 L crystalloid), respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Right shin with pain out of proportion, dusky discolouration, crepitus on palpation, sensory reduction over affected area, no dorsalis pedis pulse loss
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22 x10^9/L; Hb 128 g/L; Na 132 mmol/L; Cr 148 micromol/L (baseline 88); glucose 16 mmol/L; CRP 240 mg/L; lactate 3.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily with observation in the short stay unit for 12 hours
Urgent surgical review for operative debridement with concurrent IV meropenem, vancomycin and clindamycin
IV flucloxacillin 2 g four times daily alone with elevation and outpatient review in 24 hours
MRI of the affected leg first to confirm the diagnosis before considering any surgery
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy as the primary intervention before surgery or antibiotics

stem:
A 42-year-old woman with primary adrenal insufficiency on maintenance hydrocortisone 20 mg mane and 10 mg mid-afternoon plus fludrocortisone 100 microgram daily is brought to the emergency department by her partner. She has had gastroenteritis for 36 hours with vomiting and profuse watery diarrhoea. She has been unable to keep down her morning hydrocortisone dose for the last two mornings and has not used her emergency hydrocortisone injection.

On arrival she is drowsy, confused and hypotensive. Blood tests show sodium 122 mmol/L, potassium 5.8 mmol/L, urea 12.2 mmol/L, creatinine 118 micromol/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L. Her ambulance BP was 82/54 mmHg. She has been given 1 L normal saline in transit with modest response. There is no fever and she has no meningism.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 88/58 mmHg after 1 L saline (initial 82/54), respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, orientated to person only; dry mucous membranes; capillary refill 3 seconds; no focal neurology

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Oral hydrocortisone 40 mg immediately with anti-emetic and observation for the next 2 hours
IV fludrocortisone 200 microgram daily as the primary steroid replacement for the crisis today
IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus and 200 mg per 24 hours infusion with continued fluid resuscitation and glucose
IV dexamethasone 4 mg bolus and reload with oral hydrocortisone when she can tolerate it
IV prednisolone 25 mg bolus and delay definitive replacement until adrenal axis testing has been completed

stem:
A 52-year-old man presents with 4 days of ascending symmetrical lower limb weakness, now involving his hands. He had a diarrhoeal illness 2 weeks ago that resolved spontaneously. On examination he has 3/5 power in both legs, reduced deep tendon reflexes globally, and mild bilateral facial weakness. His forced vital capacity is 1.6 L (predicted 4.5 L), and his single breath count is 12. His swallow is intact and he has no autonomic instability.

A lumbar puncture shows CSF protein 1.2 g/L, WCC 4 cells/microL (<5), glucose 3.8 mmol/L (blood 5.2). Nerve conduction studies were requested and are pending. He is otherwise well with no comorbidities. He has been admitted to the neurology high-dependency bay.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Bilateral 3/5 lower limb weakness; upper limb 4/5; areflexia; mild facial diplegia; sensory pinprick reduced distally; intact swallow; no autonomic instability
data_table.Investigations: FVC 1.6 L (predicted 4.5); single breath count 12; CSF protein 1.2 g/L (<0.45); CSF WCC 4 cells/microL (<5); glucose 3.8 mmol/L (blood 5.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immunotherapy plan?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 60 mg daily with taper over 8 weeks and no other immunotherapy
IV rituximab 1 g single dose targeting B-cell mediated autoantibody production as the sole intervention
Observation only with physiotherapy input and no immunomodulatory therapy as the sole intervention
IV immunoglobulin 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days with respiratory function monitoring and ventilation preparation
IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days as first-line to hasten recovery as the sole intervention

stem: You are the ICU registrar assessing a 68-year-old woman admitted 6 hours ago with fever, dysuria and hypotension after 2 days of urinary sepsis. She initially responded to 30 mL/kg crystalloid and IV gentamicin plus ampicillin. She is now deteriorating despite noradrenaline at 0.4 microgram/kg/min; her BP has fallen to 82/48 mmHg, urine output has dropped to 10 mL/hour and lactate has risen from 3.4 to 5.2 mmol/L. Her ECG shows new T-wave inversion in V4 to V6, JVP is elevated 6 cm above sternal angle, and there are new fine bibasal crackles on auscultation. Bedside echocardiogram shows moderately reduced LV systolic function (EF 30 percent, prior TTE 6 months ago was normal) with no significant valve lesion or pericardial effusion. Troponin is 480 ng/L (<20) rising from 60 ng/L 4 hours ago. Point-of-care ultrasound of the IVC shows a distended 2.4 cm IVC with less than 30 percent respiratory variation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg on noradrenaline 0.4 microgram/kg/min, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 92 percent on 6 L via mask, temperature 37.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Cool clammy peripheries; JVP 6 cm above sternal angle; new fine bibasal crackles; S3 gallop; peripheral oedema absent
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 5.2 mmol/L (rising from 3.4); troponin 480 ng/L (baseline <20, rising from 60); ECG anterolateral T inversion; TTE EF 30 percent (baseline normal 6 months ago); IVC distended 2.4 cm with reduced variation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her circulatory support?

options.text: Give a further 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus and increase noradrenaline to 0.8 microgram/kg/min as the sole intervention
Add IV vasopressin 0.03 unit/min alone without any inotrope or fluid adjustment with routine outpatient follow-up
Withdraw the noradrenaline and switch to IV metaraminol 10 mg boluses as needed with routine outpatient follow-up
Give IV furosemide 80 mg alone and continue current haemodynamic support without inotrope as the sole intervention
Add dobutamine 5 microgram/kg/min IV and stop further fluid resuscitation; arrange urgent cardiology review for possible mechanical support

subtopic_detail: Endocarditis modified Duke criteria and empirical antibiotic
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 68-year-old woman on the acute medical unit with 3 weeks of malaise, unintentional 3 kg weight loss, drenching night sweats and a low grade fever. She had a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement 4 years ago for severe calcific aortic stenosis. She has no intravenous drug use history and no recent dental work. She lives in inner Perth.

On examination she is unwell but not septic. There is a soft ejection systolic murmur in the aortic area unchanged from her clinic notes and a new small area of petechiae on her right conjunctiva; no other embolic signs and no splinter haemorrhages. Chest is clear. Abdomen is soft with no tenderness. Two sets of blood cultures taken 12 hours apart both grow Streptococcus sanguinis, and a transthoracic echocardiogram today shows a 6 mm vegetation on the bioprosthetic aortic valve leaflet with mild valvular regurgitation. She has no penicillin allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 38.1 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Soft ejection systolic murmur aortic area, small right conjunctival petechial patch, no splinter haemorrhages, no splenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Two sets of blood cultures 12 hours apart both positive for Streptococcus sanguinis; transthoracic echocardiogram 6 mm vegetation on bioprosthetic aortic valve with mild regurgitation; CRP 82 mg/L (<10); WCC 10.4 x10^9/L; creatinine 78 micromol/L

lead_in: Which regimen best meets Australian empirical treatment for her prosthetic valve endocarditis while susceptibilities are pending?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily with rifampicin 300 mg twice daily as an outpatient management plan
Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g every 4 hours as monotherapy for a total treatment duration of 6 weeks
Intravenous vancomycin 25 mg per kilogram every 12 hours plus rifampicin 600 mg oral twice daily for 6 weeks
Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g every 4 hours plus gentamicin 1 mg per kilogram every 8 hours for 2 weeks
Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours plus gentamicin 1 mg per kilogram every 8 hours

stem:
You are the general medical registrar reviewing a 34-year-old man born in Vietnam who moved to Australia at age 18. He is being worked up in your outpatient clinic for adalimumab therapy for severe Crohn's disease not responding to azathioprine. He is otherwise well and has no cough, weight loss, night sweats or contact with active tuberculosis in the last year. His BCG vaccination scar is visible on his left deltoid from childhood. He has no HIV and is not on other immunosuppressants.

Pre-treatment screening includes a chest radiograph reported as clear with no evidence of prior granulomatous disease. His QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus (QFT-Plus) assay returns positive with TB1 antigen minus nil of 1.6 IU/mL and TB2 antigen minus nil of 1.9 IU/mL (positive cut-off 0.35 IU/mL or higher). Baseline sputum microscopy and Xpert MTB/RIF are negative on three morning samples.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No lymphadenopathy, chest clear on auscultation, no clubbing
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph clear; QFT-Plus TB1 1.6 IU/mL and TB2 1.9 IU/mL (positive cut-off 0.35 or higher); sputum microscopy and Xpert MTB/RIF negative x 3; HIV negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management step before starting adalimumab?

options.text: Proceed with adalimumab now because BCG history explains a false positive QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus result
Commence rifampicin plus isoniazid plus pyrazinamide plus ethambutol for 6 months for active pulmonary tuberculosis
Repeat the QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus assay in 6 months and defer adalimumab until then to observe for indeterminate result
Perform tuberculin skin test to confirm latent tuberculosis before initiating any treatment given prior BCG vaccination
Start isoniazid 300 mg daily plus pyridoxine 25 mg daily for 9 months for latent tuberculosis before adalimumab initiation

stem:
You are the medical registrar in a metropolitan emergency department. A 74-year-old man is brought in by ambulance with a 24-hour history of confusion, poor oral intake and rigors. He was recently discharged after a 5-day admission for community-acquired pneumonia treated with intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin. His usual medications are ramipril, metformin and rosuvastatin.

On arrival he is sleepy but rousable, with warm peripheries and a productive cough. Chest examination reveals crackles at the right base. Blood cultures have been taken and intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g plus gentamicin 5 mg per kilogram have already been given within the first hour. He has received 30 mL per kilogram of intravenous crystalloid over the last 60 minutes. Despite this his blood pressure remains 82/48 mmHg, mean arterial pressure 60 mmHg, with ongoing tachycardia and rising serum lactate from 4.2 to 5.1 mmol/L (0.5-2.2).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, MAP 60 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 94 percent on 4 L nasal prong, temperature 39.1 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Sleepy but rousable, warm peripheries, productive cough, right basal crackles, urine output 20 mL in the last hour
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 5.1 mmol/L (0.5-2.2) rising from 4.2 mmol/L; WCC 21 x10^9/L; CRP 340 mg/L; creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 90 micromol/L); Hb 128 g/L; blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Commence noradrenaline infusion titrated to a target mean arterial pressure of 65 mmHg or higher
Give a further 30 mL per kilogram intravenous crystalloid bolus over 30 minutes before commencing vasopressor
Add intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg daily as continuous infusion for septic shock without vasopressor
Order urgent contrast computed tomography of chest to identify pulmonary embolism as alternative diagnosis
Commence adrenaline infusion at 0.05 microgram per kilogram per minute as first-line vasopressor for septic shock

stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man in the emergency department with 24 hours of left leg pain and redness. He has type 2 diabetes on metformin (last HbA1c 8.4 percent). He recalls no obvious skin breach but scraped the shin on a garden edge 3 days ago. The pain has become severe out of proportion to the skin appearance and he is now unable to weight bear.

On examination there is erythema extending from the shin proximally to mid-thigh with tenderness far beyond the erythema margins. The overlying skin has a dusky purple hue in the centre with early bullae. Crepitus is not palpable but there is marked oedema. He is diaphoretic and confused. Bloods show WCC 22 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 380 mg/L (<10), sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 88), glucose 18 mmol/L, haemoglobin 128 g/L (135-175). His LRINEC score is calculated at 9. Plain radiograph of the leg shows no gas in the tissues.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Erythema shin to mid-thigh with tenderness beyond margins; dusky purple hue with early bullae centrally; marked oedema; unable to weight bear
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22 x10^9/L (4-11); CRP 380 mg/L (<10); sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145); creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 88); glucose 18 mmol/L; Hb 128 g/L (135-175); LRINEC 9; plain radiograph no soft-tissue gas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 hours and reassess clinical progress in the next 24 hours
Urgent surgical consultation for exploration and debridement with broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics
Order urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the leg before deciding on antibiotic or surgical intervention
Give a therapeutic dose of enoxaparin subcutaneously to cover the possibility of an occlusive vascular event
Discharge with oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily and mark the erythema for review in 48 hours

stem:
You are the general medical registrar in an endocrinology outpatient clinic reviewing a 46-year-old woman with 18 months of progressive central weight gain of 14 kg, easy bruising, proximal myopathy and new-onset hypertension. Her old photos show a rounder face and buffalo hump. She has type 2 diabetes newly diagnosed 6 months ago and now takes metformin 1 g twice daily. She has not been on any oral, topical or inhaled steroid.

On examination she has round facies, prominent supraclavicular fat pads, several purple striae on her abdomen and thighs greater than 1 cm wide, thin skin with easy bruising and proximal muscle weakness. She has no galactorrhoea, no visual field defect, and abdominal examination is otherwise unremarkable. She has never been on oral contraception. Recent bloods show HbA1c 8.9 percent, potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), and morning cortisol 720 nmol/L. She works day-shift and sleeps regularly. She does not drink alcohol.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 164/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Round facies, supraclavicular fat pads, purple abdominal striae over 1 cm wide, proximal muscle weakness, no galactorrhoea, no visual field defect
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 8.9 percent; potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); morning cortisol 720 nmol/L (140-620); no exogenous glucocorticoid exposure

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line screening test for Cushing syndrome in this patient?

options.text: 8 am plasma ACTH measurement to differentiate ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome
High-dose 8 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test as initial screen for ACTH-dependent disease
1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test with 8 am cortisol measurement the following morning
Pituitary MRI with contrast to look for a corticotroph microadenoma as the primary diagnostic test
24-hour urinary catecholamines and metanephrines to exclude phaeochromocytoma before Cushing syndrome workup

stem:
You are the on-call medical registrar. A 62-year-old woman with polymyalgia rheumatica on long-term prednisolone 7.5 mg daily for 3 years is brought in by her husband with 24 hours of profuse watery diarrhoea, vomiting and progressive lethargy. She stopped her prednisolone 3 days ago because she could not keep it down. She has no other medications. She has no known adrenal insufficiency diagnosis but has not had a Synacthen test.

On arrival she is drowsy and cool peripherally. Capillary refill is 4 seconds. Her tongue is dry and eyeballs are sunken. Bloods show sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-6.0), urea 12 mmol/L, creatinine 128 micromol/L (baseline 68). A random cortisol taken on arrival is 90 nmol/L. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.28, HCO3 18 mmol/L, base excess minus 8, lactate 3.4 mmol/L. Blood pressure is not responding adequately to a 500 mL bolus of intravenous saline. ECG shows sinus tachycardia only.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, dry tongue, sunken eyes, cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145); potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-6.0); urea 12 mmol/L; creatinine 128 micromol/L (baseline 68); random cortisol 90 nmol/L; VBG pH 7.28, HCO3 18, base excess minus 8, lactate 3.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.2)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Give intravenous fludrocortisone 100 microgram bolus alongside continued intravenous crystalloid resuscitation
Withhold steroid until a formal short Synacthen test confirms adrenal insufficiency before administering hydrocortisone
Restart oral prednisolone at 7.5 mg immediately and provide antiemetic to control ongoing vomiting
Give intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus and start intravenous 5 percent glucose in saline resuscitation
Commence intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg every 6 hours as it does not interfere with a subsequent Synacthen test

subtopic_detail: Ectopic ACTH from small cell lung cancer
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 62-year-old man on the acute medical unit. He was admitted 3 days ago with severe hypokalaemia at 2.6 mmol/L and metabolic alkalosis after collapsing at home. He has smoked 30 cigarettes a day for 40 years. He has lost 8 kg over 3 months and reports increasing shortness of breath. He has no history of steroid use.

On examination he is thin with truncal wasting rather than obesity, and has hyperpigmentation of the palmar creases and buccal mucosa. There is no purple striae, no round facies, and no supraclavicular fat pads. He has proximal muscle weakness. Blood pressure remains 168/98 mmHg despite potassium replacement. Investigations show 24-hour urinary free cortisol 5 times upper limit of normal, 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test cortisol 480 nmol/L (does not suppress under 50), and plasma ACTH 380 ng/L (10-50). High-dose 8 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test shows cortisol falling by only 20 percent from baseline. Chest radiograph shows a 3 cm right hilar mass.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 168/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 94 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Thin build with truncal wasting, hyperpigmented palmar creases and buccal mucosa, no purple striae, proximal muscle weakness
data_table.Investigations: 24 h urinary free cortisol 5x upper limit; 1 mg overnight DST cortisol 480 nmol/L (does not suppress below 50); ACTH 380 ng/L (10-50); high-dose 8 mg DST cortisol suppressed only 20 percent; K 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2) after replacement; VBG pH 7.48, HCO3 32 mmol/L; CXR 3 cm right hilar mass

lead_in: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Pituitary corticotroph microadenoma causing ACTH-dependent Cushing disease with paraneoplastic lung lesion
Primary adrenal cortisol-secreting adenoma with a coincidental incidental lung nodule from smoking
Exogenous glucocorticoid use with factitious hypercortisolism and unrelated pulmonary carcinoma
Cushing disease with rapid tumour growth explaining lack of high-dose suppression and mass effect on the lung
Ectopic ACTH from small cell lung carcinoma given the hypokalaemic alkalosis, hyperpigmentation and DST failure

stem:
A 39-year-old man newly diagnosed with HIV attends your general practice for review of his baseline results. He is asymptomatic apart from mild oral candidiasis. He is starting to consider antiretroviral therapy and is anxious about opportunistic infections. He has no other medical conditions and takes no regular medications.

On examination he is well nourished. Oral thrush is confirmed on the palate. Chest is clear and there is no lymphadenopathy. Baseline results show CD4 count 180 cells/microL (500-1500), HIV viral load 92000 copies/mL, hepatitis B surface antigen negative, hepatitis C antibody negative, syphilis serology negative, Toxoplasma IgG positive, and QuantiFERON-TB Gold negative. Renal function and liver enzymes are within normal limits. He is fully immunised for age. His G6PD status is normal on screening.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Well nourished, oral candida on palate, no lymphadenopathy, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: CD4 180 cells/mcL (500-1500); HIV RNA 92000 copies/mL; Toxoplasma IgG positive; QuantiFERON-TB Gold negative; UEC and LFTs within normal limits; G6PD normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate opportunistic infection prophylaxis to commence today?

options.text: Oral azithromycin 1200 mg once weekly as Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis for the current CD4 count
Oral fluconazole 200 mg daily as primary prophylaxis against cryptococcal meningitis and oesophageal candidiasis
Oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg one tablet daily as Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis
Oral isoniazid 300 mg daily plus pyridoxine 25 mg for 9 months of latent tuberculosis treatment as the priority prophylaxis
Oral valaciclovir 500 mg twice daily as chronic herpes simplex virus suppression indefinitely while CD4 remains low

stem:
A 32-year-old nurse returns to your general practice after employer screening. She emigrated from the Philippines 4 years ago, has no known TB contact and is a healthy non-smoker on no regular medications. She has never had a chest infection and denies fever, night sweats, weight loss or productive cough. She feels well.

On examination her chest is clear, there is no cervical lymphadenopathy and vital signs are normal. Her QuantiFERON-TB Gold test is positive (interferon-gamma 1.8 IU/mL). Chest radiograph shows no infiltrate, cavitation or lymphadenopathy. HIV serology is negative. Liver enzymes are within normal limits. She wants to know whether she has tuberculosis and what should happen next.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Well, no lymphadenopathy, chest clear, no scars
data_table.Investigations: QuantiFERON-TB Gold positive (IFN-gamma 1.8 IU/mL); CXR: no infiltrate or cavitation; HIV serology negative; LFTs within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Reassure that this is a false-positive result from BCG vaccination in childhood and no further follow-up is required
Commence rifampicin-isoniazid-pyrazinamide-ethambutol quadruple therapy empirically today as directly observed therapy
Repeat the QuantiFERON-TB Gold in 6 weeks to confirm boosting phenomenon before offering any active management
Offer treatment for latent tuberculosis infection with rifampicin 600 mg daily for 4 months with monthly liver enzyme monitoring
Refer for early morning sputum acid-fast bacilli smear x3 and TB PCR before any decision about latent tuberculosis treatment

A 68-year-old woman is brought to your emergency department by ambulance with 24 hours of urinary frequency, fever and worsening confusion. She has type 2 diabetes on metformin, hypertension on ramipril and chronic kidney disease stage 3 (baseline creatinine 140 micromol/L, eGFR 42 mL/min/1.73 m^2). She lives independently and is normally alert and oriented. She has no known drug allergies.

On arrival she is confused (GCS 13/15, disoriented to time and place), warm and vasodilated, and complaining of loin pain. Cardiovascular examination shows dual heart sounds without murmur. Chest is clear. Abdomen has right renal angle tenderness. Point-of-care venous lactate is 3.6 mmol/L (0.5-2.2). Urine dipstick shows blood 2+, leukocytes 3+ and nitrites positive. Her weight is 80 kg. She has no chills currently but had rigors overnight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 88/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 96 percent on 4 L/min via nasal prong, temperature 39.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: GCS 13, warm vasodilated peripheries, right renal angle tenderness, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Venous lactate 3.6 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); urine dipstick blood 2+, leukocytes 3+, nitrites positive; creatinine 210 mcmol/L (from baseline 140)

lead_in: Within the first hour, which set of interventions best meets Australian sepsis pathway targets?

options.text: Blood cultures then intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g plus oral paracetamol and admit for further monitoring
Blood cultures then intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g and 500 mL normal saline infused over the next 4 hours as maintenance therapy alone
Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g without blood cultures because she is already on empirical antibiotics and cultures will be unreliable
Serum lactate, blood cultures then intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g and 30 mL per kilogram intravenous crystalloid over the first hour
Blood cultures and lactate, then intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g and 30 mL per kilogram crystalloid, with repeat lactate at the end of the first hour

stem:
A 46-year-old woman is brought to your emergency department by her husband with 2 days of vomiting, worsening fatigue and a 3-hour history of collapse. She has a background of primary autoimmune Addison's disease diagnosed 6 years ago, maintained on hydrocortisone 15 mg on waking and 5 mg at 2 pm plus fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily, and has autoimmune hypothyroidism on thyroxine 100 micrograms daily. She was well until 3 days ago when she developed a gastroenteritis-like illness with vomiting; she was unable to keep her steroids down but did not increase her dose or seek care.

On arrival she is pale, cold, drowsy, and profoundly hypotensive. She has skin hyperpigmentation of the palmar creases and old buccal patches consistent with Addison's. She has no focal neurology. Point-of-care venous glucose is 2.6 mmol/L (3.5-6.0). Bedside biochemistry shows sodium 122 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), urea 12 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), creatinine 148 micromol/L (45-90) and eosinophils 0.6 x10^9/L (0.02-0.5).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 74/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 35.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pale, cold, drowsy, palmar and buccal hyperpigmentation, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 122 mmol/L (135-145); potassium 5.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.5); glucose 2.6 mmol/L (3.5-6.0); creatinine 148 mcmol/L (45-90); eosinophilia 0.6 x10^9/L (0.02-0.5)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately followed by 1 litre 0.9 percent normal saline with 5 percent dextrose over the first hour
Intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg immediately with plans to perform a formal short synacthen test later this admission
Intravenous 3 percent hypertonic saline 100 mL bolus to correct her severe hyponatraemia before other measures are undertaken
Intravenous 10 units short-acting insulin with 50 mL of 50 percent dextrose to correct hyperkalaemia as first-line therapy
Oral hydrocortisone 60 mg stat with intravenous 0.9 percent normal saline 500 mL over 30 minutes and paediatric admission

A 58-year-old man is brought to your regional emergency department with 45 minutes of sudden severe tearing chest pain radiating to his back. He has poorly controlled hypertension (usual blood pressures around 165/95 mmHg), a 30-pack-year smoking history and takes amlodipine 5 mg daily. He denies drug allergies.

On arrival he is pale and diaphoretic. Cardiovascular examination shows a soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge and a blood pressure differential of 40 mmHg between arms (right 210/104 mmHg, left 170/98 mmHg). Peripheral pulses are all palpable but the left radial is weak. His neurology is intact and there is no focal weakness. Point-of-care troponin is elevated at 62 ng/L (<14). ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 118/min without acute ST changes. Chest radiograph shows a widened mediastinum. Bedside transthoracic echocardiography suggests an intimal flap in the ascending aorta and a small pericardial effusion. Cardiothoracic retrieval to the tertiary centre has been called and estimated at 45 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure right arm 210/104 mmHg, left arm 170/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98 percent on 4 L/min via nasal prong, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pale, diaphoretic, soft early diastolic murmur, 40 mmHg inter-arm BP differential, weak left radial pulse, neurology intact
data_table.Investigations: Troponin 62 ng/L (<14); ECG sinus tachycardia; CXR widened mediastinum; TTE intimal flap in ascending aorta with small pericardial effusion

lead_in: While awaiting retrieval, what is the single most appropriate initial pharmacological plan?

options.text: Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion titrated to a systolic blood pressure of 120 mmHg without any prior heart rate control agent
Intravenous esmolol infusion titrated to heart rate 60 to 80/min, then intravenous glyceryl trinitrate to systolic blood pressure 100 to 120 mmHg
Intravenous aspirin 300 mg plus intravenous heparin loading dose of 5000 units for suspected acute coronary syndrome
Intravenous hydralazine 20 mg bolus every 30 minutes titrated to systolic blood pressure below 120 mmHg without any beta blocker
Intravenous morphine 5 mg boluses titrated to pain control while awaiting retrieval, with no antihypertensive or heart rate agent

A 62-year-old woman presents to your emergency department with 4 hours of headache and blurred vision. She was diagnosed with essential hypertension 5 years ago and takes irbesartan 300 mg and amlodipine 10 mg daily, but has been non-adherent for 6 weeks due to a prescription lapse. She has no history of stroke or heart failure and does not smoke.

On arrival she is drowsy but rousable, oriented to person only. Fundoscopy shows bilateral flame haemorrhages and cotton wool spots without papilloedema. Cardiovascular examination shows an S4 gallop without S3, no pulmonary crackles and no peripheral oedema. Neurological examination shows no lateralising signs and reflexes are symmetric. Urinalysis has 2+ protein and blood. Bedside creatinine is 148 micromol/L (from baseline 84 micromol/L on record 3 months ago). Non-contrast computed tomography of the head shows no intracranial haemorrhage. ECG shows sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy criteria and no acute ischaemia.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 232/142 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, oriented to person only, no focal neurology, bilateral flame haemorrhages and cotton wool spots without papilloedema, S4 gallop
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 148 mcmol/L (baseline 84 3 months ago); urinalysis 2+ protein, 2+ blood; ECG LVH criteria; CT head no haemorrhage

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial pharmacological plan?

options.text: Oral captopril 25 mg with observation over 2 hours before considering further dose escalation or parenteral antihypertensive agents
Intravenous nifedipine short-acting 10 mg sublingual bolus for rapid blood pressure reduction to a target of 140/90 mmHg within 30 minutes
Intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus repeated every 10 minutes as needed to reduce mean arterial pressure by no more than 25 percent in the first hour
Restart irbesartan 300 mg and amlodipine 10 mg orally and observe on the ward for 48 hours before further consideration
Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate 5 microgram per minute titrated as sole agent to systolic below 120 mmHg within the first 30 minutes

A 44-year-old woman presents to your endocrinology clinic with 8 months of weight gain (12 kg), facial rounding, easy bruising, three vertebral compression fractures on recent spinal imaging and new hypertension diagnosed 4 months ago. She has type 2 diabetes for which metformin was added 2 months ago. She has no other medications. She works night shifts as a security officer and reports irregular sleep for 3 years.

On examination she has central obesity, thin bruised skin over the shins and upper limbs, and purple striae over the abdomen more than 1 cm wide. Blood pressure is 168/98 mmHg. Her random cortisol at 3 pm is 620 nmol/L (100-540). Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test: morning cortisol 210 nmol/L (target below 50). A 24-hour urinary free cortisol is 850 nmol/day (55-330). Late night salivary cortisol collected on 2 different days: 22 and 18 nmol/L (below 3 in typical circadian rhythm). Her plasma ACTH is 62 ng/L (10-60). Thyroid function, prolactin, and IGF-1 are within normal limits. She has no visual field defect.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 168/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Central obesity, thin bruised skin, purple abdominal striae >1 cm wide, blood pressure 168/98 mmHg, no visual field defect
data_table.Investigations: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression cortisol 210 nmol/L (target <50); 24-hour urinary free cortisol 850 nmol/day (55-330); late night salivary cortisol 22 and 18 nmol/L; plasma ACTH 62 ng/L (10-60)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat the 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test in 6 months given her night-shift lifestyle likely accounts for the abnormal circadian result
Non-contrast computed tomography of both adrenals to look for a unilateral adrenal adenoma before further biochemical testing
Serum aldosterone to renin ratio to screen for primary hyperaldosteronism as the explanation of her hypertension and hypokalaemia
High-dose 8 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test followed by pituitary magnetic resonance imaging if suppression occurs
Empirical trial of metyrapone 250 mg 3 times daily to reduce cortisol synthesis before further diagnostic imaging is requested

A 54-year-old man presents to your emergency department with 4 days of progressive limb weakness, initially in the arms, now involving his legs. He noted double vision on waking today and difficulty swallowing sips of water. He had a diarrhoeal illness 2 weeks ago that resolved without treatment. He has no other medical history and takes no medications.

On examination he is alert with bilateral partial ophthalmoplegia and a downbeating nystagmus on lateral gaze. Cranial nerves show weakness of eye abduction bilaterally and mild bulbar dysfunction with pooling of secretions. Limb tone is reduced, power 3/5 proximally and 4/5 distally in all limbs. Deep tendon reflexes are absent throughout. Sensation is normal to pinprick and vibration. Coordination testing shows marked truncal ataxia with inability to sit unsupported. Forced vital capacity at the bedside is 1.4 L (predicted 4.2 L). Lumbar puncture shows CSF protein 1.6 g/L (0.15-0.45), glucose 3.8 mmol/L (2.2-3.9), and 2 lymphocytes/microL (0-5). MRI brain and cervical spine are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, bilateral partial ophthalmoplegia, downbeating nystagmus, truncal ataxia, generalised areflexia, symmetric limb weakness with intact sensation
data_table.Investigations: CSF protein 1.6 g/L (0.15-0.45), 2 lymphocytes/mcL (0-5); MRI brain and cervical spine normal; forced vital capacity 1.4 L (predicted 4.2 L)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days as first-line therapy for suspected multiple sclerosis relapse presenting acutely
Intravenous edrophonium 10 mg to establish the diagnosis of myasthenic crisis by symptomatic improvement of ptosis and swallowing
Intravenous aciclovir 10 mg per kilogram every 8 hours empirically for herpes simplex brainstem encephalitis while awaiting further imaging
Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g plus dexamethasone 10 mg for suspected brainstem meningoencephalitis pending microbiology results
Intravenous immunoglobulin 0.4 g per kilogram daily for 5 days, admit to a high-dependency unit and monitor forced vital capacity 4-hourly
